title: Narrative Plenitude
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: Kurt Wootton borrows Viet Thanh Nguyen's concept of narrative plenitude, the condition in which so many stories exist about a cultural group that no single work has to define it, and applies it to how teachers choose texts. Greek myth enjoys plenitude, since students meet it in Percy Jackson, The Odyssey and modern retellings, while many groups live in narrative scarcity where a few representations harden into stereotype. He argues that adding a single book to broaden a curriculum can unintentionally reinforce scarcity, because one book cannot represent a whole people. A visit to the Museo Nacional de Antropologia in Mexico City showed him how much Mesoamerican history is missing from school curricula, which he calls narrative omission. He describes building a teacher institute around Donna Barba Higuera's novel Xolo and asks teachers to aim for abundance, so that students encounter an ever-expanding world of stories.
points: Adding one book from an overlooked perspective is not enough, because a single text cannot carry the weight of representing an entire culture.
Narrative plenitude is a goal of abundance across many versions and forms, not a checklist of representation.
The comparison between Greek and Mesoamerican myth shows how uneven a curriculum's coverage can be, which Wootton calls narrative omission.
Retellings such as Higuera's Xolo, which centers a secondary figure from the original myth, are a way to join oral storytelling traditions while widening who stories are about.
The author's own ignorance of Mesoamerican myth was the reason to build learning around it, which models teachers learning alongside students.
quotes: Narrative plenitude is when so many stories are told about a particular cultural group that no single piece of media or art needs to carry the burden of defining that group.

As educators, we sometimes unintentionally reinforce narrative scarcity in our curriculums. In our efforts to broaden what students read, we might add a book representing a perspective that has traditionally been left out.
But a single book can’t represent an entire culture or group of people. Narrative plenitude asks us to think beyond representation toward abundance.

As I wandered through the museum’s vast halls, I was struck by how much of this history is left out of our school curriculums. It’s perhaps not just an instance of narrative scarcity, but of narrative omission.
In Higuera’s more recent novel Xolo, she returns to the idea of stories worth telling by reaching back into the myths of Mesoamerica.
Many of the world’s origin stories and myths began in oral traditions. The stories that eventually became The Odyssey were told for centuries before the poem took the form that we read in print.
It is up to us, to the best of our abilities, to foster greater narrative plenitude in our classrooms, so our students experience an ever-expanding world of stories and histories.
